Mental health

Eating disorders

Anorexia, bulimia and binge-eating disorder: warning signs, treatment and the family's role.

Medical review Alejandro Rosàs, family doctor

Need help now? In Spain, 024 is free and open 24 hours; in an emergency call 112. Elsewhere, contact your local helpline or emergency services. This text is for general information: it cannot diagnose and does not replace seeing a professional.

What they are

Eating disorders are serious health problems in which a person's relationship with food, weight and body image is persistently disturbed, affecting physical and psychological health. The main ones are:

  • Anorexia nervosa: restricted eating leading to significantly low weight, intense fear of gaining weight and distorted perception of one's own body. It is among the mental disorders with the highest mortality rates.
  • Bulimia nervosa: episodes of bingeing (eating a large amount with a sense of loss of control) followed by compensatory behaviour such as vomiting, laxatives, fasting or excessive exercise. Weight is usually normal, which makes it harder to detect.
  • Binge-eating disorder: repeated binges without compensatory behaviour, with distress and guilt. It is the most common.
  • Others, such as avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID), in which foods are avoided because of texture, fear of choking or lack of interest, without concern about weight.

They usually begin in adolescence or early adulthood and are more common in women, but they also affect men and people of any age, weight or social background.

What they are not

They are not a fad or a choice, and they are not diagnosed by weight alone: someone of normal or high weight can have a serious eating disorder. Dieting is not a disorder, though restrictive diets are a risk factor.

Warning signs

  • Rapid weight loss or, in adolescents, failure to gain expected weight.
  • Skipping meals, eating in secret or going to the bathroom right after eating.
  • Compulsive exercise.
  • Loss of periods, dizziness, constantly feeling cold.
  • Intense preoccupation with shape and weight, constant mirror-checking or weighing.

How they are assessed

They require a medical assessment (weight, vital signs, blood tests, an ECG where indicated) as well as a psychological one, because physical complications can be serious. Questionnaires such as the SCOFF help detect cases in primary care.

Which interventions are studied

  • In children and adolescents with anorexia, family-based treatment (the Maudsley model), in which parents temporarily take charge of eating, is the first choice.
  • In adults, enhanced cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT-E) and other specialist therapies.
  • For bulimia and binge eating, cognitive behavioural therapy, including guided self-help.
  • Nutritional care, medical monitoring and, in severe cases, day hospital or admission.

How to seek help

If you suspect a problem, see the paediatrician or family doctor. The earlier it is treated, the better the outlook. Family associations offer guidance and support.

How to support someone

Speak from concern, not criticism: "You look tired and I'm worried". Avoid comments about weight or bodies, yours or anyone else's. Don't turn every meal into a battle; seek professional support for the family.

Myths to avoid

  • "It only affects thin young women". It affects any sex, age and weight.
  • "It's a matter of willpower". It is a disorder with biological, psychological and social roots.
  • "The family is to blame". Families do not cause the disorder and are an essential part of treatment.

References

  1. Treasure, J., Duarte, T. A. y Schmidt, U. (2020). Eating disorders. The Lancet, 395(10227), 899–911.
  2. National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (2017). Eating disorders: recognition and treatment (NG69). Londres: NICE.
  3. Morgan, J. F., Reid, F. y Lacey, J. H. (1999). The SCOFF questionnaire: Assessment of a new screening tool for eating disorders. BMJ, 319(7223), 1467–1468.
  4. Arcelus, J., Mitchell, A. J., Wales, J. y Nielsen, S. (2011). Mortality rates in patients with anorexia nervosa and other eating disorders: A meta-analysis of 36 studies. Archives of General Psychiatry, 68(7), 724–731.
